title: Authentication, authorization, and session boundaries
sources: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard concepts: authentication and authorization
Python documentation: secrets and hmac module concepts
masterChecklist: API design and consumption: validation, authentication concepts, status codes, pagination, versioning
Input validation, injection risks, deserialization, path traversal, secrets, dependency risk, safe subprocess use
Threat modelling, trust boundaries, secure defaults, secure code review, incident triage
whyItMatters: A user being signed in does not mean they may read or change every record. Many serious application failures come from checking identity once and forgetting to enforce ownership/permission at the exact operation that touches data.
simpleExplanation: Authentication answers ‘who is this?’ Authorization answers ‘may this identity do this action on this resource?’ A session or token carries an identity claim between requests, but the service still validates it and checks permission at each protected boundary.
mentalModel: Showing a ticket at a building entrance proves you entered the building. It does not automatically open every office. Each restricted door checks whether your badge grants access there.
outcomes: Distinguish identity proof from permission checks.
Place authorization beside the protected resource/action.
Use generic public errors without exposing private record existence.
Keep secrets out of source code and logs.
Recognize that framework/session details vary and must be implemented with the selected framework's documented controls.

realWorldExample.scenario: A learner requests a progress record by ID through a web API.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: The API checks that any learner is logged in but fetches any supplied record ID. Changing the ID exposes another learner's progress.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Resolve a verified current identity, load the resource through an ownership/role-aware query or check, return a safe refusal when not permitted, log only safe audit context, and test both allowed and denied cases.

explanation: The example keeps the permission rule close to the protected record.
It compares a verified current-user identity with resource ownership; a real service may additionally check roles, teams, or organization scope.
The denied response is intentionally generic here to avoid revealing whether a private record exists. Product/legal requirements may require a different documented policy.
The code is a teaching rule, not a complete login/session implementation. Production identity verification belongs in a well-reviewed framework/identity boundary.
Tests should cover both the allowed and denied path for every protected operation.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Remove the permission check and see why any signed-in user could read the record. Then add a role field and write a clearly documented admin exception.

procedure: Identify assets, identities, actions, and trust boundaries before writing routes or handlers.
Use a reviewed authentication boundary to establish the current identity; do not trust a user ID supplied as an ordinary request field.
At each protected read/change, check ownership, role, organization scope, and any business-state rule needed for that action.
Return safe errors that do not disclose private data beyond the policy.
Store secrets in an appropriate secret/configuration mechanism; never put passwords, keys, or raw tokens in source, browser storage without a design review, or ordinary logs.
Write allowed and denied tests for every sensitive action.
Review session expiry, logout/revocation, rate limits, audit trails, and framework-specific protections as part of the selected deployment design.

commonMistakes.mistake: Checking only that a request is authenticated.
commonMistakes.why: An authenticated identity may still be unauthorized for the specific resource.
commonMistakes.avoid: Enforce authorization at the resource/action boundary.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trusting an account ID from the URL/body as the acting user identity.
commonMistakes.why: A caller can change that value.
commonMistakes.avoid: Obtain the acting identity from verified authentication context, then compare it with the target resource.

commonMistakes.mistake: Logging raw tokens or passwords to help debugging.
commonMistakes.why: Logs are commonly retained and widely accessible during incidents.
commonMistakes.avoid: Log safe identifiers/outcomes and redact secrets by design.

lab.title: Protect a local progress record with an ownership rule
lab.safety: Uses local dictionaries only. It does not implement login, tokens, encryption, or network access.
guidedSteps: Treat current_user_id as a value supplied by a trusted authentication layer for this simulation.
Compare it to record['learner_id'] in one permission function.
Return a safe refusal for a different user.
Copy/update only on the allowed path.
Write one allowed and one denied assertion.
checks: Separates ownership rule from update behavior.
Does not mutate the record on a denied request.
Explains that real authentication is outside this local simulation.
lab.solutionExplanation: The ownership test occurs before the update. The allowed result creates a new record value, so the original local input remains unchanged. A real service must verify the current identity using its configured authentication system before applying this rule.
challenges: Predict the risk if can_edit always returns True for any signed-in user.
Find the bug: comparing current_user_id to a record ID rather than record owner ID.
Experiment: add a documented admin role without making every user an admin.

projectConnection.milestone: Add an ownership/role decision function and tests for permitted and refused progress reads/updates. Add a short threat-boundary note naming what the local project simulates and what a real deployment must provide.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: Every protected action has an explicit authorization rule, denied attempts do not mutate data, test cases cover both outcomes, and no secrets appear in source or example logs.

assessment.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
assessment.answer: Authentication establishes an identity; authorization decides whether that identity may perform a specific action.
assessment.explanation: Both are required for protected resources.

assessment.question: Why should permission be checked near the resource action?
assessment.answer: That is where the service has the actual target/ownership context and can prevent bypass through another route.
assessment.explanation: A broad login check alone is insufficient.

assessment.question: Why avoid raw tokens in logs?
assessment.answer: Logs can expose retained secrets to people or systems that should not possess them.
assessment.explanation: Use safe identifiers and redaction instead.
